Governance & provenance
Every event carries its provenance — which feed it came from, whether that feed is live or a frozen sample, and when it arrived. The exposure history shows what moved on the book over time (when a footprint updates, you see what changed and when). The alert record is the permanent, append-only log of who was told what. Everything here is governed and auditable.
Loading governance…
Event Radar — the unstructured sensor (we knew before the satellite)
The official feeds are reliable but lagging — a wildfire is often in the news hours before the satellite confirms it. Event Radar scans a real live disaster feed (GDACS) and news wires, picks out the peril, place and severity, and checks it against the book: does it touch homes we insure, and has an official feed caught it yet? A "beats the feed" signal is an early warning. The scan is automatic; promoting a signal into a live event — which pushes it into the exposure view and the alerts — is a human decision, kept on record. Nothing consequential happens on its own.

Live event — follow a developing wildfire, and stop a sale you shouldn't make
A wildfire breaks in the news hours before the satellite confirms it. Start following the story and the map redraws as the fire spreads — more insured homes fall inside, the exposure climbs, and the satellite catches up to confirm it. Meanwhile a customer whose home the fire is reaching tries to buy cover: the system declines it on the spot — you can't insure a home that's already in an active fire zone. The agent explains why, and an underwriter can override. Every decision is kept on record. (Illustrative synthetic story; the distance check is real.)

Data sources & quality — what we ingest, how fresh it is, and what we refused
Every hazard feed we rely on, in one place: what it carries, whether it's real-time, a batch, or a frozen sample kept for a reproducible room, when it last arrived and how many records came in. Every pull passes a quality gate before it can touch the book — if a batch fails a check (for example, too many records outside Europe), it is rejected and quarantined and the previous good data stays in use. 1 · How it works

From a catastrophe to a decision

Nine steps, each one a governed function or table you can open.

“When a fire starts, I need three answers fast: which of our homes are in the path, what it could cost us after reinsurance, and who needs to know. Then I need to stop selling cover in that zone.” — an exposure manager
1
Trust the data

The insured property book (3_property) carries a geocoded location for every insured home — the same policy spine the rest of the estate uses.

2
Find the footprint

An event footprint (2_event_footprint) arrives from a hazard feed — wildfire perimeter, flood extent, storm warning area — after passing the quality gate. Multi-part events are joined into one shape.

3
Measure the exposure

fn_exposure_in_footprint intersects homes with the footprint using Databricks geospatial SQL in a metre-true projection (EPSG:3035), so 50 / 100 / 200 m are real metres; inside the footprint counts as 0 m.

4
See it whole — across borders

fn_event_exposure_summary rolls the same rows up by distance band and by country, so one event shows its whole cross-border exposure — no country silos.

5
Net of reinsurance, and by coverholder

fn_gross_to_net turns the sum insured at risk into a modelled loss (ref_damage_factor) and runs it through the Property Cat XL programme to what we keep; fn_exposure_by_coverholder splits it by delegated authority.

6
Tell the people who aren't logged in

When an event crosses its threshold, fn_event_delta works out what's new since the last look and one alert per event goes to claims, underwriting and exposure management — every dispatch kept in gov_alert_dispatch.

7
Follow it live — and refuse anti-selection

A developing fire is followed as it spreads (2_event_progression); at the same time fn_bind_check declines cover on a home inside the active zone, and the underwriting workbench uses fn_zone_check the same way for UK flood warnings. Every decision is recorded.

8
Ask in plain English

A supervisor agent routes questions to six specialists; each answers only by calling governed functions. Genie answers ad-hoc questions over the book and shows its SQL.

9
Govern & trust

Every feed is quality-checked and logged (gov_feed_dq_log), every event carries provenance (gov_data_provenance), exposure history is time-travelable (gov_exposure_history) and every alert and bind decision is append-only.

2 · Architecture

One governed platform, end to end

Feeds come in on the left; decisions go out on the right. Everything in between lives in Unity Catalog.

Built from standard Databricks pieces
  • Lakeflow Jobs (serverless) pull each feed on a schedule, with retry and back-off; a streaming ingest (Auto Loader) shows records arriving live.
  • Delta tables in Unity Catalog hold raw pulls, footprints, the insured book and every audit log — with lineage, permissions and history.
  • Governed SQL functions do all the maths (geospatial, gross → net, bind checks). The app, the agents and the dashboards all call the same functions, so the numbers agree everywhere.
Consumed in many places
  • This app and AI/BI dashboards (the maps).
  • Alerts — a scheduled job emails the right people.
  • AI agents on Agent Framework, using the functions as tools through a managed MCP server.
  • Genie for ad-hoc questions, and the underwriting workbench, which checks active zones at bind.
  • Everything scales to zero when no one is using it.

Cadences as configured in this demo; the jobs are scheduled in production and run on demand in the room. A rejected batch never reaches 2_event_footprint — it goes to 1_feed_quarantine and the previous good data stays in use.

4 · Theory

Cat-modelling basics

Every catastrophe estimate, from a spreadsheet to a full cat model, combines the same four ideas.

  • Hazard — where the event is and how intense it is (a fire perimeter, a flood depth, a wind speed).
  • Exposure — what we insure, and exactly where: location, sum insured, construction, occupancy.
  • Vulnerability — how much damage a given intensity causes, expressed as a damage ratio (share of the sum insured lost).
  • Financial terms — deductibles, limits and reinsurance, which turn the ground-up loss into gross and net.
Loss ≈ Σ (sum insured × damage ratio at that home's hazard intensity), then apply policy terms and reinsurance.

This workbench keeps the vulnerability deliberately simple and visible: a damage factor per peril and distance band (ref_damage_factor). Distance stands in for intensity — embers carry, flood depth falls away — and 50 / 100 / 200 m are the client's own thresholds.

Accumulation is the total we have inside one footprint. It's the concentrations, not the averages, that hurt — which is why the board counts homes in the path, not portfolio totals.

What a full cat model adds: thousands of simulated years of events (a stochastic event set), uncertainty around each damage estimate, and the outputs capital and reinsurance work with — exceedance-probability curves (occurrence and aggregate), average annual loss, and return-period losses such as 1-in-200. A vendor or open-source model (for example Oasis LMF) can write its results into the same tables; the workbench stays the place where live events meet the book.

5 · Regulation

Solvency II natural catastrophe risk, and why reinsurance matters

Capital is held against a 1-in-200-year loss; catastrophes are one of its largest drivers for a property insurer.

  • The calibration. The Solvency Capital Requirement is set at the 99.5% value-at-risk over one year — a 1-in-200-year bad outcome (Directive 2009/138/EC, Article 101).
  • Where catastrophe risk sits. It is part of the non-life underwriting risk module. In the standard formula, the non-life catastrophe risk sub-module covers natural catastrophes (windstorm, earthquake, flood, hail and subsidence) and man-made catastrophes, including a fire test based on the largest concentration of buildings within a 200 m radius (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/35). Firms can use an approved internal model instead.
  • Reinsurance reduces the charge. Recognised risk-mitigation such as a catastrophe excess-of-loss (Cat XL) programme reduces the net loss in a catastrophe and so the capital needed. Here the programme keeps the first €25m and cedes layers above it up to €400m — exactly what the gross → net card computes.
  • Your own view (ORSA). The own risk and solvency assessment (Directive 2009/138/EC, Article 45) expects the firm's own view of its risks, including perils the standard formula handles only indirectly, such as wildfire, and stress and scenario tests.
Why the 200 m matters twice: the client's 200 m alert band and the standard formula's fire-concentration test are the same idea — know where your biggest cluster is.

References at the level of the regulation; the workbench's figures are illustrative and not a capital calculation.

6 · Practice

Exposure-management practice — what good looks like

The disciplines a London-market or European exposure team is expected to run, and where each shows up here.

  • Realistic Disaster Scenarios (RDS). Lloyd's asks managing agents to estimate their gross and net losses under prescribed extreme scenarios (for example a European windstorm or a UK flood). It is the same question this workbench answers for a live event: what does this footprint cost us, gross and net?
  • Accumulation control. Aggregates by peril and zone, monitored against appetite limits continuously — not once a year. The alert thresholds are that control made automatic.
  • Event response. When an event develops: find the exposed policies, estimate the loss, tell claims, reinsurance and management, and keep tracking as it evolves — then stop writing new business in the zone.
  • Delegated-authority oversight. Risk written by coverholders under binders must be visible to the insurer in time to act — hence the exposure split by coverholder.
7 · Data, licensing & climate

Open data you can use — and the obligations that come with it

Most live hazard data is free and open, but each source has terms, and location data about people is personal data.

SourceTerms of use
Copernicus (EFFIS, EMS, GloFAS)EU free, full and open data policy; attribute Copernicus.
NASA FIRMSOpen NASA Earth-science data; attribute NASA FIRMS.
MeteoAlarmRe-use under MeteoAlarm / EUMETNET terms, with attribution.
GDACSFree use with attribution (UN and European Commission).
Environment AgencyOpen Government Licence v3.0 — “Contains Environment Agency data”.
  • GDPR. A precise location linked to a policyholder is personal data. Use it for a lawful purpose (the contract), keep only what you need, and control access — Unity Catalog row filters and column masks do this per role. This demo uses synthetic data only.
  • Climate. Wildfire seasons in southern Europe are lengthening and heavy-rainfall floods are becoming more frequent. EIOPA expects insurers to assess climate risk in the ORSA, including with scenarios where material, and the CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464) brings climate disclosure under ESRS E1 — the same physical-risk data feeds both.
